**ua-parser-js — four hours in which `npm install` fetched a cryptominer (2021)**

On 22 October 2021 an attacker took over the npm account of the maintainer of ua-parser-js, a small library that works out which browser and device a visitor is on from their user-agent string. Hardly anyone chooses it deliberately, yet it was downloaded around eight million times a week and sat inside the dependency tree of over a thousand other packages. Three tampered releases stayed live for roughly four hours.

What made those hours dangerous was not the library code. Each release carried an install script, which npm runs automatically the moment a package lands on your machine. It checked whether it was on Windows or Linux, then launched a shell script or batch file that installed a cryptocurrency miner. On Windows it also dropped a credential stealer that went after browser cookies and saved passwords. Nobody had to import the library. Installing was enough, and advisories told affected developers to treat every credential on the machine as compromised. Rapid7 reported that the maintainer's account had no two-factor authentication.

That is what `npm install` actually is: a command that downloads code from strangers, pulls in whatever that code depends on, and lets it execute on your machine before you have written a line. Nothing here asks you to stop using npm — you cannot build a full-stack project without it. It asks you to know what the command does. Read what you are adding, keep `package.json` and its lockfile honest so you can see which versions you installed, and treat an unexplained dependency the way you would an unexplained email attachment.

**Twitter — the day tweet IDs grew too large for JavaScript to count (2010)**

In 2010 Twitter moved to a new identifier scheme called Snowflake, which packs a timestamp, a machine number and a counter into a 64-bit number. Twitter announced the change on its developer mailing list months ahead, because it broke one group of developers in particular: some languages — JavaScript above all — cannot hold a whole number that large.

JavaScript has a single number type. `42` and `3.14` are the same kind of thing, both stored as a 64-bit floating-point value. That format holds whole numbers exactly only up to 9,007,199,254,740,991, which is two to the power of 53 minus one. Past that, values round to whatever can be represented. There is no error and no warning: you hand the parser a nineteen-digit ID, you get a number back, and the last digits are quietly wrong. An identifier wrong in its final digits is not a close match — it is a different tweet, or none.

Twitter's fix was to publish every ID twice. Alongside the numeric `id`, responses gained an `id_str` field holding the same value as a string, which no parser rounds. String versions appeared from 22 October 2010; IDs crossed the 53-bit threshold that November, after which the numeric field was unusable from JavaScript. The API still returns both.

This lesson tells you JavaScript has one number type. Here is why that sentence earns its place. Anything you handle as an identifier — a database key, an order reference, an ID from someone else's API — belongs in a string unless you have checked it fits. The same care applies to money: hold amounts in whole pence, so a value never rounds behind your back.

**FirstEnergy — the alarm that stopped without saying so (2003)**

On 14 August 2003 a cascading power failure swept across the north-eastern United States and Ontario, leaving an estimated 55 million people without electricity. Investigators kept returning to a control room in Ohio, where operators at the utility FirstEnergy watched a screen that had quietly stopped telling the truth.

Their alarm and event processing ran on General Electric's XA/21 system, whose code contained a race condition: two parts of the program could write to the same shared data at the same moment, and when a burst of events arrived in the wrong order the program locked into an infinite loop. The alarms stopped, and nothing on the display said so. Operators saw a calm board while transmission lines sagged into trees and dropped out one after another. The Register reported that engineers took some eight weeks to find the fault, slowing the software down and injecting delays to reopen a window only milliseconds wide.

Two things belong to this lesson. The first is the race. JavaScript's single thread spares you two threads writing one variable at the same instant, but not the underlying problem: every `await` is a point where your function stops and other work runs, so two requests that read a value, wait for a database, then write it back can interleave and lose one another's change.

The second is the silence. That alarm system did not crash; it failed while still looking fine. A promise that rejects with nobody listening behaves the same way. Catching rejections, and wrapping `await` calls in `try`/`catch`, is how you make a failure say something instead of leaving you watching a calm board.

**Steam — the cache that served one shopper another shopper's account page (2015)**

On Christmas Day 2015, Steam users loading the store began seeing pages belonging to strangers. Valve's account, published on 30 December, set out the sequence: the store was under a denial-of-service attack that drove traffic up by around 2,000 per cent, and a caching configuration was deployed through Steam's web caching partner to absorb it. During a second wave a further configuration went out that cached responses generated for logged-in users.

A cache holds a copy of a response and hands it to the next person who asks for that URL. That is fine for a product image and catastrophic for an account page, because the URL for "your account" is the same for everyone — the difference is carried in the request, not the address. Valve stated that roughly 34,000 accounts had pages served to other people, exposing billing addresses, purchase histories, email addresses and the last digits of a card number and a phone number. Full card numbers and passwords were not exposed, and nobody could log in as an affected user. Valve took the store down for about an hour.

This is the request lifecycle from your lesson failing at a point beginners rarely think about. HTTP is stateless, so a response is personal only because the request that produced it carried an identity — a session cookie or an `Authorization` header. Anything between client and server that reuses responses has to be told that, through headers: `Cache-Control: private` or `no-store` on anything user-specific. When you build an API, decide for every response whether it is safe to reuse and say so. A cache will not work it out for you.

**Uber — an access key left in a code repository (2016)**

In the autumn of 2016 intruders reached Uber's cloud storage using an access key an engineer had committed to a GitHub repository. The repository was private, and that was no protection. The US Federal Trade Commission's account describes how they got in: Uber let engineers reach company repositories through personal accounts, did not stop them reusing passwords, and did not require multi-factor authentication. The intruders logged in with passwords exposed in other companies' breaches, read the key out of the source, and used it.

According to the FTC they downloaded sixteen files of unencrypted personal data — roughly 25.6 million names and email addresses, 22.1 million names and mobile numbers, and 607,000 driving licence numbers. Uber paid the attackers $100,000 through its bug bounty programme and did not disclose the breach for over a year. It later paid $148 million to settle with US state attorneys general, and its former security chief was criminally convicted over the concealment.

No clever exploit was involved. A credential was typed into a file, the file was committed, and the commit was permanent. Git is a history, not a folder: deleting a secret in a later commit leaves it sitting in the earlier one, readable by anyone who clones the repository — and a private repository today can be published, forked or breached tomorrow.

That is why this lesson puts `.env` into `.gitignore` before you write your first line of configuration rather than after. Ignore `node_modules` and `.env` from the first commit, and if a key ever does reach a repository, treat it as public and rotate it.
